newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour oozes confidence as election nears.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour oozes confidence as election nears.

text.p: Ten days on from "Wobbly Thursday" when his campaign suddenly looked as if it might veer off the road, Labour leader Tony Blair is back on cruise control.

With just 10 days to go to Britain's May 1 election, Labour's campaign is exuding confidence and Blair himself has loosened up as the finishing line that he hopes will end 18 years of Conservative rule heaves into view.

Challenging a reporter to a game of video soccer, as he did during a visit to a software company in Manchester on Monday, might not be a defining political moment. The same is true of when he tossed his failed microphone to the floor during a rally in Edinburgh last Thursday and had to shout to be heard.

But they are the sort of spontaneous gestures he was shying away from earlier in the campaign, before he realised that a cramped, safety-first approach could open the door to a Conservative fightback.

Blair is not taking any more political risks, but in a presidential-style campaign where style is as important as substance, he is injecting more passion into his performances to counter charges that his party, having dumped its socialist baggage, no longer believes in anything.
The Labour leader, of course, has been helped by a new outbreak of civil war in the ruling Conservative party over Britain's role in Europe.
"The obvious truth can be avoided no longer: if the Conservatives win this election, they cannot form a successful government.

"That isn't a statement of party-political bias: it is the only logical conclusion that can be drawn from the past few days of election camapaigning," Andrew Marr, editor of the Independent newspaper, wrote on Monday.

Blair's aides, wary of premature triumphalism, refuse to take victory for granted and even grumble disingenuously that the focus on Conservative infighting has prevented Labour from getting its positive messages on health and education across.
But there is almost a blinking disbelief that the commanding poll lead the party has enjoyed for the past three years shows little sign of crumbling.

"We thought the polls would have narrowed by now," one of Blair's close associates said, adding that Labour's own polling gives it a double-digit lead over the Conservatives. Published polls put the lead at 14 to 19 percentage points.
Labour will now work in the next week to ensure that its supporters turn out in force on May 1.

There will be a particular emphasis on getting out the young vote, which presumably explains why Blair, fresh from a keynote speech on foreign policy in the northern city of Manchester, spent part of the morning being grilled by Kev, a disc jockey from a local rock radio station.

They were not the sort of questions that Blair will be expected to answer if he gets to 10 Downing Street. How long do your drinking sessions last? Which supermodel would you like a one-night stand with? "Ha ha!" laughed Blair.

The Labour leader obliged by naming his favourite football team (Newcastle) and the actor he would you like to portray you on film (Ralph Fiennes, star of the English Patient), but drew a line when Kev asked whether he ironed his own underpants and picked his nose.
"Now Kev," said the would-be prime minister, "I think you've gone a bit far."
